events.title: Solar flare!
events.text: A burst of particles from the Sun hits the spacecraft in 2 hours. Radiation can scramble unprotected electronics.

choices.label: Safe mode
choices.hint: Switch instruments off for a day

outcomes.log: Instruments off. Flare passed. All systems nominal.
outcomes.why: Safe mode protects electronics. One lost day is a tiny price.

choices.label: Keep working
choices.hint: Don't lose a day of science

outcomes.log: Main computer glitched. Backup computer took over.
outcomes.why: Your redundancy kit's backup computer saved the mission.

outcomes.log: Instrument electronics damaged. Data quality down 15%.
outcomes.why: Radiation damaged unprotected electronics. Safe mode would have cost only one day.

events.title: Antenna pointing error
events.text: The antenna drifted off Earth. Reboot the pointing system (uses 20% of power for a week) or keep going and hope it holds?

outcomes.log: Reboot complete. Antenna locked on Earth.
outcomes.why: You had spare power, so the reboot cost nothing. Power margin is insurance.

outcomes.log: Reboot done, but instruments had to pause for a week.
outcomes.why: Without spare power, the reboot paused the science. A power margin of 20% avoids this.

outcomes.log: Backup pointing sensor holds the lock on Earth.
outcomes.why: The redundancy kit's backup sensor fixed the pointing.

outcomes.log: Pointing keeps drifting. Data rate down 30% for the rest of the mission.
outcomes.why: A tiny pointing error means much of the radio beam misses Earth.

events.title: Entry, descent and landing
events.text: Seven minutes from the top of the atmosphere to the ground. The signal takes longer than that to reach Earth, so the lander is on its own.

outcomes.log: Heat shield glowing at 1,300 °C... parachute out... rockets firing... TOUCHDOWN!
outcomes.why: The heat shield let the air slow you down from 20,000 km/h.

outcomes.log: Signal lost during entry. The spacecraft burned up in the atmosphere.
outcomes.why: No heat shield: air friction heated the spacecraft to over 1,000 °C. Landers on Mars must carry one.

events.title: Powered descent
events.text: No air to slow down, so the engine fires all the way to the ground.

outcomes.log: Engine burning... 100 meters... 10 meters... contact light. TOUCHDOWN!
outcomes.why: With no air, every bit of braking comes from fuel. That's why landers are so heavy.

events.title: Orbit insertion
events.text: The main engine must fire at exactly the right moment, or the spacecraft flies past.

outcomes.log: Main engine burn complete. We are in orbit!
outcomes.why: Braking into orbit needs a long engine burn: that's the extra fuel mass you carried.

events.title: Closest approach
events.text: The spacecraft races past at thousands of km/h. Every instrument fires at once.

outcomes.log: Closest approach: 300 km above the surface. Instruments recording.
outcomes.why: A flyby needs no braking fuel, but the close-up view lasts only hours.

events.title: Radiation dose climbing!
events.text: Close passes give the sharpest data, but Jupiter's radiation is eating the electronics.

outcomes.log: Shielding holds. Sharp data, some wear on the electronics.
outcomes.why: Backup electronics let you take the risk. Europa Clipper hides its electronics in a thick vault.

outcomes.log: Electronics degrading fast. Expected mission life cut in half.
outcomes.why: Radiation slowly destroys computer chips. Without shielding or backups, the mission dies early.

outcomes.log: Passes widened. Slightly blurrier data, much safer spacecraft.
outcomes.why: Trading a little science for a much longer life is often the smart engineering choice.

events.title: Sunset
events.text: The lunar night begins: 14 Earth days of darkness at −170 °C.

outcomes.log: Solar power at zero. Battery drained. The lander froze.
outcomes.why: Solar landers cannot survive the 14-day lunar night. An RTG keeps them warm.

events.title: Dust storm!
events.text: Dust blocks the Sun. Power from your panels just dropped by 60%. Not enough to run everything.

choices.label: Hibernate
choices.hint: Turn instruments off, keep heaters on

outcomes.log: Instruments asleep for 6 weeks. Heaters on. The lander survived the storm.
outcomes.why: Saving power kept the electronics warm. The rover Opportunity was lost in a storm like this in 2018.

outcomes.log: The battery carried the lander through the darkest days.
outcomes.why: The battery stored energy for exactly this kind of bad day.

outcomes.log: Heaters failed. Electronics froze at −80 °C. Mission over early.
outcomes.why: Without enough power for heaters, electronics freeze. An RTG doesn't care about dust.

events.title: Dust storm!
events.text: A planet-wide dust storm blocks the Sun.

outcomes.log: RTG output unchanged. All systems nominal.
outcomes.why: Your RTG doesn't need sunlight, so the dust storm changed nothing.

events.title: Global dust storm
events.text: Dust hides the whole surface for two months. Your orbiter is safe above it, but the cameras can't see the ground.

choices.label: Study the storm
choices.hint: Point the instruments at the atmosphere

outcomes.log: Instruments studying the storm itself. Rare atmosphere data!
outcomes.why: A flexible plan turns bad luck into new science.

choices.label: Wait it out
choices.hint: Pause and wait for clear skies

outcomes.log: Two months of waiting. Surface mapping resumes after the storm.
outcomes.why: Waiting is safe, but two months of instrument time were lost.

events.title: Memory full!
events.text: Instruments make more data than the antenna can send home. The onboard memory is full.

choices.label: Compress data
choices.hint: Smaller files, a bit less detail

outcomes.log: Compression on. 25% more science now fits through the link.
outcomes.why: Squeezing files lets a slow antenna send more, at a small cost in detail.

outcomes.log: Oldest data deleted to make room.
outcomes.why: Data that can't be sent is lost. A bigger antenna fixes the root cause.
